messages.subject: HMM for animal movement spending too long in each state
parts:
Hello,

I have been working with a HMM model where animal movement (distance moved, and relative angle) depends on a latent state. The first state is 'foraging' where the animal moves short distances, and frequently changes its movement direction between steps. The other state is 'migrating' where the animal moves with purpose in a given direction, characterised by long steps and small changes in its relative angle.

Bob very kindly helped us to get a model up and running using dynamic programming. I have been comparing this model with fake data, to see how it fares. At the moment the model seems to be (quite strongly) overestimating the time spent in state 1 (Bob mentioned this in his original posting of the model.) For some reason the switching probabilities for state 2 appear to be estimated fairly faithfully.

My question is: is there anything we can do to remedy this issue?

At the moment we have tried the following:

a. Setting priors for the switching probabilities that are concentrated towards 0.5. This helps a bit, but the priors need to be very concentrated for us to get estimates that are close to the true values.
b. If instead we supply the true switching probs as data, we still see that the estimated latent vector tends to get stuck. 
c. Supplying (as data) the true values for rho, alpha and mu, and using the resultant model to estimate the latent state vector. It still seems to get stuck in a given state!

Does anyone have any other ideas? I include the model below:

functions{
  ## Function that returns the log pdf of the wrapped-Cauchy
  real wrappedCauchy(real aPhi, real aRho, real aMu) {
    return(- log(2*pi()) + log((1-aRho^2)/(1+aRho^2-2*aRho*cos(aPhi-aMu))));
  }
  
}


data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] phi;
  vector<lower=0>[N] l;
  int<lower=1> K;
  vector<lower=0>[K] theta_priors;
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[K]; ## Switching parameter
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[K] mu; ## Location of wrapped Cauchy
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[K] rho; ## Scale of wrapped Cauchy
  positive_ordered[K] alpha; ## Exponential parameters
}  
model {
  vector[K] log_theta[K];
  vector[K] lp;

  for (k in 1:K) log_theta[k] = log(theta[k]);
  lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K); ## Initial state log-probability
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K)
      lp[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta[k] + lp)
        + wrappedCauchy(phi[n], rho[k], mu[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(l[n] | alpha[k]);
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);

  alpha[1] ~ normal(0.001,0.0001); ## Priors concentrated near to true values
  alpha[2] ~ normal(0.005,0.0001);

  ## Supply theta prior parameters as data
  for(i in 1:K){
    theta[i] ~ dirichlet(theta_priors);
  }
  
}


generated quantities {
  int<lower=1,upper=K> y_star[N];
  real log_p_y_star;
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
    for (k in 1:K)
      best_logp[1, K] = wrappedCauchy(phi[1], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(l[1] | alpha[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
      best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;
          logp = best_logp[t-1, j]
          + log(theta[j, k]) + wrappedCauchy(phi[t], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(l[t] | alpha[k]);
          if (logp > best_logp[t, k]) {
            back_ptr[t, k] = j;
            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }
    }
    log_p_y_star = max(best_logp[N]);
    for (k in 1:K)
      if (best_logp[N, k] == log_p_y_star)
      y_star[N] = k;
      for (t in 1:(N - 1))
      y_star[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      y_star[N - t + 1]];
  }
}

I found the same thing during simulation using a von Mises
distribution for the change in direction.

I wonder if it may have to do with the fact that if we
set up a constrained variable

real<lower = - pi() / 2, upper = pi() / 2> theta;

that there's a discontinuity, because in terms of angles,
pi()/2 == -pi()/2.

I'm curious what happens with simulated data in packages
like moveHMM, which I would assume suffer the same problem,
because I saw the same thing with optimization in Stan.

I'm pretty sure the coding of the HMM isn't the issue.

- Bob

Yes. There's an implicit uniform prior on unit vectors,

to increment the log density with the log Jacobian determinant
of the transform.

- Bob

functions{
  ## Function that returns the log pdf of the wrapped-Cauchy
  real wrappedCauchy(real aPhi, real aRho, real aMu) {
    return(- log(2*pi()) + log((1-aRho^2)/(1+aRho^2-2*aRho*cos(aPhi-aMu))));
  }

## Function that returns a random sample from wrapped-Cauchy by first
  ## sampling from the Cauchy, then using modular arithmetic
  real wrappedCauchy_rng(real aRho, real aMu){
    real aCauchyRand;
    real aWCRand;
    
    aCauchyRand = cauchy_rng(pi()+aMu,-log(aRho));
    if (aCauchyRand>0){
      aWCRand = fmod(aCauchyRand,2*pi()) - pi();
    } else{
      aWCRand = -fmod(-aCauchyRand,2*pi()) + pi();   
    }

    return(aWCRand);

}
  
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()>[N] phi;
  vector<lower=0>[N] l;
  int<lower=1> K;
}

parameters {
  simplex[K] theta[K];

unit_vector[2] xy[K];  // xy[1]^2 + xy[2]^2 = 1
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[K] rho;
  positive_ordered[K] alpha;
}  
transformed parameters{
  real<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()> mu[K];
  for(i in 1:K){
    vector[2] aXY;
    aXY = xy[i];
    mu[i] = atan2(aXY[1], aXY[2]) - pi();

}
  
}

model {
  vector[K] log_theta[K];
  vector[K] lp;

  for (k in 1:K) log_theta[k] = log(theta[k]);
  lp = rep_vector(-log(K), K); ## Initial state log-probability
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K)
      lp[k]
        = log_sum_exp(log_theta[k] + lp)
        + wrappedCauchy(phi[n], rho[k], mu[k])
        + exponential_lpdf(l[n] | alpha[k]);
  }
  target += log_sum_exp(lp);

  alpha[1] ~ normal(0.001,0.0001);

alpha[2] ~ normal(0.005,0.0001);
  rho[1] ~ normal(0.95,0.01);
  rho[2] ~ normal(0.3,0.01);

}

  int<lower=1,upper=K> y_star[N];
  real log_p_y_star;
  {
    int back_ptr[N, K];
    real best_logp[N, K];
    real best_total_logp;
    for (k in 1:K)
      best_logp[1, K] = wrappedCauchy(phi[1], rho[k], mu[k])
                      + exponential_lpdf(l[1] | alpha[k]);
    for (t in 2:N) {
      for (k in 1:K) {
      best_logp[t, k] = negative_infinity();
        for (j in 1:K) {
          real logp;

            best_logp[t, k] = logp;
          }
        }
      }

      y_star[N] = k;
      for (t in 1:(N - 1))
      y_star[N - t] = back_ptr[N - t + 1,
      y_star[N - t + 1]];
  }

parts:
What I found in running multiple chains is that they
did indeed converge, but the label-switching problem remains.
The ordering of means for the distance traveled indeed identified
this simple model. But, you have to be aware that doing the
ordering changes the model's posterior (perhaps not significantly,
but I'm not sure how to test that without doing things Andrew
won't approve of).

For locking in particular observations in an HMM, do you mean
something like assuming it always starts in state 1 or something
like that? We could code that, and it won't change the model.
I'm not sure how well it'll identify things given the long-running
chains. It doesn't seem to work so well with ideal-point models.

- Bob
